COVID-19: SA State of Readiness amid Escalating Infections

By: Mosibudi Ratlebjane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at the state of preparedness of health system amidst the increasing Covid-19 Infections in South Africa.

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa saw the pandemic much later than other countries, like Spain, Italy and the US. Unfortunately, the easing of strict lock-down regulations has brought about a rapid infection rate, with patients rushing into hospitals for medical assistance and making South Africa the country with the highest number of Covid positive cases on the continent. Marking over 100 days of Lock-down in South Africa,the pressing question we ask is, how effective was the lockdown in getting South Africa’s health system adequately prepared to deal with the scores of people needing tests, hospitals beds and the necessary skill to get them back to health.

Summary:
By interviewing two main experts, with slightly opposing viewpoints. We will be able to answer this question about the why there are conflicting views, where experts differ in their projections of infections rates and the effectivity of the lockdown in preparing the health system


Prof Salim Abdool Karim, (he had a more positive outlook on what the lockdown could do for the health sector and reduce the number of infections.

“South Africa will see outbreaks of new infections, after the national lockdown, it’s going to happen whether we like it or not. The key thing is not to get worked up about it. You know what to expect, you know it’s coming, and when you see it, we’ll put it in place [ways to mitigate it”.]

Professor Shabir Madhi
While the lockdown has bought time for South Africa’s health system to prepare, wrong timing, a lack of testing, the wrong type of testing and the slow release of results had snatched away government’s chances to significantly slow community infections



Further information:
The Story:
This story looks at the three factors: Testing, Medical Staff, and the infrastructure needed to sufficiently handle the pandemic. What did the three month lockdown do? And how well prepared is the South African Health system, how effective was the lockdown?

- Testing
- Medical Staff
- Infrastructure.

By zoning in one the hospital in the Ekurhuleni municipality, Tembisa Hospital: designated as the Covid hospital in Gauteng, serving a population of 3.8 Million in the East Rand area. We use this Hospital as a microcosm of what may be happening in the our public hospitals.
It may seem that the initial lockdown was not sufficient time to prepare for the peak of the Covid-19 infections.

Case Studies:
Shoni’s Lethols Death, at the Tembisa Hospital has made national news, creating a spotlight with the state of readiness, public facilities are in Shoni Lethola, a 34 year old male, complained about chest and back pains, before calling his father to get medical assistance. Upon Arriving at Three Different Hospitals within the East Rand area, Shoni was referred to Tembisa Hospital, where his father requested a wheelchair for his son. Shoni’s was taken into the casualty ward, in which he witnessed other patients dying in front of him.
A tweet sent two days after his admission into the hospital. Shoni addressed the Minister of Health, telling the Minister that he had not eaten in two Days. the nurses. It so happens that Shoni also complained to his family about not being able to walk to the bathroom. And that the nurses were not helping them.

Case Study:
Nicola Ncube Nicol Ncube’s mother was admitted in the Tembisa Hospital with a preexisting condition- cancer. She was discharged and a month later, went back to Tembisa hospital, where she was immediately, said to be a Covid-19 Case without being tested. Nicols Mother Stevey, recalls her mother not receiving food, and having to share a bed with five other Covid- Patients in the wards, as there are no - adequate beds. Stevey dies on Monday but Nicol, and her sister were only told, on Friday last week.

Whistle Blower Doc - Tembisa Hospital Doctor:
A doctor working in the Causality, at Tembisa Hospital, Willing to speak about the real life experiences faced in the Covid Wards:
According to the doctor there are two doctors on call for a 12 hour Shift catering to all the Covid-19 Wards. That house about 73 patients at a time, as that is the capacity of the Wards. Medical records of patients are taken outside the wards, while the few nurses on call, refuse to entire the wards not more than twice a day in the beginning of their shifts and at the end. No one is able to assist patients to access bathrooms or food.
There are 18 Male Wards, and 28 female Wards for Covid. One more Ward has been allocated since Shoni's death created media attention.


We will Answer the Below Questions:
•Burning issue that needs to be addressed: Why are Wits experts say around 1 million but we have about 200 000 – what is this based on? Are the numbers significantly more and are these stories about ie Tembisa show that this is baring out now in healthcare?
•What’s the deal with test kits – are they reliable? Are we getting more false negatives\false positives which are exacerbating the situation.
•What is the scientific impact of these backlogs on the actual specimen taken from the patients?
• Karim - At this point were you expecting this current number of 150000 or 1 million?
• How bad is the bad log in public healthcare and how long is it actually taking for people to get results?
• Are doctors seeing more patients with in respiratory distress than what the numbers actually reflect?
• MR – At Tembisa the test takes about a week – they’ve spoken to a private lab and they are able to get tests within 24-48 hours. Story will show cause and effect.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We look at the state of preparedness of health system amidst the increasing Covid-19 Infections in South Africa.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa saw the pandemic much later than other countries, like Spain, Italy and the US. Unfortunately, the easing of strict lock-down regulations has brought about a rapid infection rate, with patients rushing into hospitals for medical assistance and making South Africa the country with the highest number of Covid positive cases on the continent. Marking over 100 days of Lock-down in South Africa,the pressing question we ask is, how effective was the lockdown in getting South Africa’s health system adequately prepared to deal with the scores of people needing tests, hospitals beds and the necessary skill to get them back to health.
metadata.Summary: By interviewing two main experts, with slightly opposing viewpoints. We will be able to answer this question about the why there are conflicting views, where experts differ in their projections of infections rates and the effectivity of the lockdown in preparing the health system Prof Salim Abdool Karim, (he had a more positive outlook on what the lockdown could do for the health sector and reduce the number of infections. “South Africa will see outbreaks of new infections, after the national lockdown, it’s going to happen whether we like it or not. The key thing is not to get worked up about it. You know what to expect, you know it’s coming, and when you see it, we’ll put it in place [ways to mitigate it”.] Professor Shabir Madhi While the lockdown has bought time for South Africa’s health system to prepare, wrong timing, a lack of testing, the wrong type of testing and the slow release of results had snatched away government’s chances to significantly slow community infections
metadata.Further information: The Story: This story looks at the three factors: Testing, Medical Staff, and the infrastructure needed to sufficiently handle the pandemic. What did the three month lockdown do? And how well prepared is the South African Health system, how effective was the lockdown? - Testing - Medical Staff - Infrastructure. By zoning in one the hospital in the Ekurhuleni municipality, Tembisa Hospital: designated as the Covid hospital in Gauteng, serving a population of 3.8 Million in the East Rand area. We use this Hospital as a microcosm of what may be happening in the our public hospitals. It may seem that the initial lockdown was not sufficient time to prepare for the peak of the Covid-19 infections. Shoni’s was taken into the casualty ward, in which he witnessed other patients dying in front of him. A tweet sent two days after his admission into the hospital.
